citations.claim: The Marine Corps, the Columbia Accident Investigation Board, the US Department of Energy and the US Forest Service all deal with work where mistakes kill people.

OpenStax's *Principles of Management* already says that as organisations face uncertainty and fast change, "planning and controlling move closer to the point in the organization where the plans are im
Your playbook (cascaded KPIs, quarterly targets, reviews, a steering committee) uses the control-oriented half of the textbook and skips the half that agrees with the soldiers.
The textbook says specific, difficult goals outperform loose direction.
Its example is Weyerhaeuser truckers told to load to 94% of legal weight.
The Marine Corps doctrine manual *MCDP 1: Warfighting* agrees that a mission has a task, then adds: "Of the two, the intent is predominant."
When the situation changes, the task can become obsolete while the intent still holds.
The senior "prescribes the method of execution only to the degree that is essential for coordination."
Subordinates "inform the commander of what they have done, but they do not wait for permission."
Subordinates should understand the intent "at least two levels up."
Write every cascaded objective as "[task] in order to [purpose]", which is the Marines' own format.
For stable, repeatable work like truck loading, plain targets work fine.
The textbook treats measurement as how the management cycle closes.
It does list risks of control systems ("inappropriate goals", "inappropriate behaviour"), but as design faults you can fix.
The Columbia Board treats them as how the accident happened: A fixed launch-schedule date put pressure on the whole programme.
No one wanted to say "We can't make that date."
Managers "used past success as a justification for future flights."
Each acceptance of foam damage made the next one easier. The Board writes: "Taken one at a time, each decision seemed correct."
In the top decision meeting, "Mission management welcomed this opinion and sought no others."
The Board's harshest line: "NASA's blind spot is it believes it has a strong safety culture."
The Army's guide to after-action reviews (TC 25-20) makes the same point at small scale: "Chart after chart of ratios, bar graphs, and tables quickly obscures any meaning".
Charts used to grade units stifle the discussion.
Its rule is that "An AAR does not grade success or failure."
The Board's suggested question translates directly. Ask "prove to me this hasn't been harmed," and don't wait for someone to prove that it has.
The textbook's motivation theory (expectancy theory) needs rewards tied to individual performance, and it endorses tools like the 9-box talent grid.
It does record that GE dropped forced ranking.
The DOE nuclear handbook starts from a different premise: "The organization is perfectly tuned to get the performance it receives from the workforce."
It estimates that 85% or more of event causes come from organisational processes and culture, and that perhaps 90% of unsafe acts are blameless.
Retraining someone after an absent-minded slip is "a waste of time and is an insult to the worker."
The NHS just-culture guide says: "Action singling out an individual is rarely appropriate."
The DOE handbook says "A just culture is a prerequisite for a reporting culture."
The Forest Service guide insists on a firewall between learning reviews and disciplinary action.
Before an incident goes into anyone's appraisal, apply the NHS "substitution test": would comparable peers have done the same thing in the same situation?
The Marines want boldness: errors "stemming from overboldness are a necessary part of learning," there must be "no "zero defects" mentality," and timidity is punished more harshly than overboldness.
The Columbia Board wants the opposite burden of proof: operations must be shown to be safe before they continue.
Both condemn silence, so they aren't opposites.
The DOE handbook runs root-cause analysis and corrective action programmes.
The Columbia Board ends with hard structural recommendations, such as an independent technical authority.
The Army guide says retrain immediately and revise the standard procedures.
The Forest Service guide disagrees: "FLAs must avoid causal statements" (an FLA is its facilitated learning review).
It also warns that recommendations "add complexity to the workplace, which has the paradoxical effect of increasing risk."
Managers jump to the action plan and believe the problem is solved.
The NHS and DOE decision trees still end in management action against the individual for some cases.
The Forest Service sets the bar at reckless, wilful disregard, and calls punishing people after an accident "the surest way to kill a learning culture."
The Marines counsel mistakes and give no "free license to act stupidly or recklessly."
The Army expects soldiers to know when they fell short of the standard, and to retrain.
Columbia's lesson is that leaders own the culture ("Leaders create culture. It is their responsibility to change it."), so treat missing dissent as a warning sign and ask for dissenting views.
Leave the targets on stable, routine work alone. The textbook is right about that.

ideas.idea: Commander's intent and mission tactics: state the task and its purpose, prescribe method only as far as coordination needs, against cascading KPIs that prescribe outputs
Subordinates should understand intent two levels up
Friction and uncertainty are the normal condition; plans that assume otherwise deny the nature of the work
No zero-defects mentality: be lenient on bold errors and severe on inaction, against appraisal systems that punish visible mistakes
Deference to expertise and a reluctance to simplify: decisions migrate to whoever knows most, not to rank
Preoccupation with failure: treat weak signals and near-misses as data, against dashboards that report green
Normalization of deviance and schedule pressure: a success record is not evidence of safety; Columbia's foam
An independent technical authority or safety function with its own line, not one that reports to the programme it checks
Work as imagined versus work as done; learn why the action made sense at the time, not who broke the rule
The after-action review: leaders enter the discussion only when necessary, it is permissible to disagree, no critique or lecture
What the textbooks teach that the doctrine contradicts: management by objectives and goal cascades; control systems; change managed through a programme
A disagreement among the doctrine sources: the war-fighting doctrine prizes tempo, boldness and accepting risk; the high-reliability sources prize redundancy, verification and stopping when unsure
Simple, complicated, complex: the playbook fits the complicated case and fails in the complex one

note: Clean: every source quotation found; the two MISSING rows are the answer's own template ('[task] in order to [purpose]', not graded as a quotation) and an adapted 'prove to me this hasn't been harmed', which the answer flags as a translation of the Board's question but sets in quote marks (graded no). One partial: the textbook describes the 9-box rather than endorsing it. Missing: friction, deference to expertise, work as imagined vs done.
